Title: The Tanzanian Educator Who Conquered Cambridge
NewsSummary: Minza brings data science and coaching skills back to Tanzania for real community impact
NewsContent:
​​​When Minza Muhandagani, an educator and health professional from Chalinze District Council, Tanzania, boarded a plane to the United Kingdom in July 2024, she was embarking on what would become a life-changing journey. Supported by the Aga Khan University’s Institute for Educational Development, East Africa (IED, EA), Minza joined the prestigious University of Cambridge Summer Programme. This four-week experience brought together learners from across the world to explore new ideas, challenge perspectives, and build bridges between disciplines. 

At Cambridge, Minza immersed herself in an intellectually vibrant environment. She took courses reflecting her dual passions for healthcare and education, including Introduction to Autism, Data Science with a Focus on Healthcare, Psychology and Coaching Practices. She immediately saw the practical applications of her studies.  

“This opportunity has enriched my knowledge and strengthened my ability to serve learners and communities more effectively,” she shared. “Courses like Data Science in Healthcare showed me how analytics can improve education and health outcomes, while Psychology and Coaching Practices gave me tools to better support and mentor students.” 

Her learning extended far beyond the lecture hall. Minza attended more than 21 plenary sessions featuring leading global academics on topics ranging from climate change to the future of technology. A visit to Bletchley Park, the historic home of British codebreakers, was unforgettable. “Seeing the machines used by Alan Turing and his team brought history to life,” she reflected. “It reminded me that great breakthroughs come from collaboration, creativity, and persistence values that are just as vital in healthcare and education today.” 

Minza embraced the full Cambridge experience, exploring historic colleges and sampling international cuisines. But it was the sense of global community that stood out most. “The diversity of ideas and backgrounds made every conversation meaningful,” she said. “It taught me that learning doesn’t stop in the classroom; it happens through every interaction.” 

Returning home, Minza is driven by a renewed sense of purpose. She plans to integrate insights on autism and coaching to enhance her support for students and patients, and to apply foundational data science skills to improve evidence-based practices in her district. “This experience has given me not only new knowledge but also a new mindset, one of curiosity, empathy, and innovation,” she said with a smile.  

Minza’s journey is a powerful demonstration of AKU’s commitment to fostering global learning and empowering East African professionals to bring back ideas that inspire change at home.
